passage: At the Monday meeting of the small architecture firm in Edinburgh, Martin clicked to the slide Freya had been dreading: the new layout for the library courtyard. "We found a way to fit twenty more bike racks without losing the tree," he said. Freya knew who "we" was. She had watched Oskar, the intern, stay till nine on Thursday, redrawing it five times with cold coffee beside him. Now Oskar sat at the end of the table, looking at his hands. The partners nodded. "Nice work, Martin." Freya's pulse picked up. She wasn't the confrontational type. But she raised her pen. "That courtyard solution is Oskar's, isn't it? I saw the Thursday drafts. Oskar, could you walk us through how you kept the tree?" A small pause. Martin said, "Yes, of course, Oskar did the drawings." Oskar looked up, surprised, and began to explain. The next week, Martin opened his slides with, "Oskar's idea, first."

qa.q: How many more bike racks did the new layout fit?
qa.a: Twenty more bike racks.

qa.q: How was Freya feeling before she spoke up?
qa.a: Freya felt nervous, her pulse picking up, since she wasn't the confrontational type.

qa.q: What made Freya's move effective?
qa.a: She named the real author calmly, backed by the Thursday drafts, and invited Oskar to explain instead of accusing Martin.

qa.q: How might Oskar have felt when Freya spoke?
qa.a: Oskar likely felt surprised and relieved, going from staring at his hands to explaining his own work.

grounding: Shows a teammate who sees a junior's work presented by someone else and quietly names the real author, shifting how credit is given.

passage: In the small meeting room at the logistics startup, Sahil sat across from Zubin, the HR manager, with a glass of water he hadn't touched. The offer was lower than he'd hoped. His lowest acceptable number was written in his notebook, face down. He didn't say it. "I've led the Pune warehouse for two years," he said. "I cut dispatch errors by a third. I'd like the offer to reflect that." Fair, and true. Zubin tapped his pen. "Do you have other offers?" Sahil's mouth opened. A friend had told him just last night: say another company offered more, they always match. The words were right there. His stomach turned. There was no other offer. If they called his bluff, or found out later, he'd be the guy who lied on day one. "Not right now," he said. "But I know what the role is worth, and I'm asking for this." He named a number above his floor. Zubin sighed, then smiled. "Let me talk to the founders."

qa.q: What did Sahil say he had cut by a third?
qa.a: Dispatch errors.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling when Zubin asked about other offers?
qa.a: Sahil felt tempted but uneasy, his stomach turning at the idea of inventing an offer that didn't exist.

qa.q: Which parts of Sahil's approach were fair bargaining?
qa.a: Keeping his lowest number private, arguing firmly with true results, and naming a number above his floor, all without lying.

qa.q: How might Zubin see Sahil's honest answer?
qa.a: Zubin may respect the honesty and firmness, and trust Sahil more as a future colleague, even while still negotiating.

grounding: Shows a person negotiating salary who keeps a bottom line private and argues firmly, and who refuses to invent a rival offer.

passage:
Wednesday night
Final round at the consultancy today. Then Divyansh, the hiring manager, slid a paper across and said, "We need your answer by 6 p.m. Honestly, people would kill for this role." It was 4:15. My palms were soaking. The salary was good, but there was a line about a "bond period" I didn't understand, and relocation "as needed".
Everything in me wanted to sign just to make the pressure stop. I felt ungrateful even hesitating. Then I remembered Didi saying: if they won't give you time, that tells you something too.
So I said, "Thank you, I'm very interested. Could you email me the full terms, including the bond clause? I'll reply by Friday noon." Divyansh looked irritated, then said, "Fine, Friday." Fine! That easily.
The email came at 7. The bond is two years with a penalty. I'm reading it with Didi tomorrow before I decide anything.
Arnab

qa.q: What time did Divyansh want an answer by?
qa.a: By 6 p.m.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when the deadline was given?
qa.a: Arnab felt pressured and anxious, palms soaking, even ungrateful for hesitating, and wanted to sign just to end the pressure.

qa.q: Why was asking for the terms by email a fair response?
qa.a: It gave Arnab time and a written copy to understand the bond and relocation lines, and showed the deadline could move.

qa.q: What might Divyansh's quick agreement to Friday suggest?
qa.a: It suggests the 6 p.m. deadline was pressure more than a real limit, and that the company still wanted Arnab.

grounding: Shows a person told an offer expires within hours and that others would kill for the job, who asks for time and written terms.

passage: Bao had run his small café in Hanoi for three years when he finally met Abebe, the coffee exporter, at a trade fair in Da Nang. Bao could have played it cool. Instead he said plainly, "I can't pay more than I pay now, this year. I'm a small shop. But I want your beans for a long time, not one order." Abebe raised an eyebrow. "Most buyers pretend they have five other suppliers." "I have one other, and theirs are worse," Bao laughed. "What matters most to you?" Abebe thought. "Steady orders. Our farmers need to know in advance." They sat over two cups for an hour. In the end Bao agreed to a fixed monthly order for two years, and Abebe offered a price Bao could manage, rising a little each year. They wrote it down together. A year later, when a drought pushed prices up everywhere, Abebe's shipments to the café still arrived on time.

qa.q: Where did Bao meet Abebe?
qa.a: At a trade fair in Da Nang.

qa.q: How did Abebe seem to feel about Bao's honesty?
qa.a: Abebe seemed surprised and intrigued, raising an eyebrow, since most buyers pretend to have many suppliers.

qa.q: What made the deal work for both of them?
qa.a: Bao explained his real limits and asked what mattered to Abebe; a fixed monthly order for two years gave the farmers steady orders and Bao a price he could manage.

qa.q: What would change if Bao had bluffed about five suppliers?
qa.a: Abebe might have held back or charged more, and the trust that kept shipments coming through the drought might never have formed.

grounding: Shows a negotiator explaining needs truthfully, asking what matters to the other side, and building terms that work for both and last.

passage: Irfan, you know me as the rule-follower, right? So listen. Last year, when Amma's hospital bills came in, I was short at the end of the month. I had a client trip to Coimbatore. The taxi was four hundred; on the claim form I wrote seven hundred. I told myself it was borrowing. I'd work extra and put it back somehow, next month. And honestly, in our office everyone rounds up. That's what I kept saying: everyone does it. The strange part is how easy the second time was. And the third. My hand didn't even hesitate. By March I had a little ledger in my head of what I owed the company, and it kept growing. Then our new manager said casually, "We're doing a sample audit of travel claims." My whole body went cold. That night I couldn't sleep. It wasn't the audit. It was realising that I, Kalyani, had become someone who needed an audit to stop. The next morning I asked to meet her.

qa.q: What did the taxi actually cost, and what did Kalyani claim?
qa.a: The taxi was four hundred; Kalyani wrote seven hundred.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the audit was announced?
qa.a: Kalyani went cold with fear, and that night felt shaken to see how far the so-called borrowing had gone.

qa.q: What turning point could stop the slide, and what should Kalyani do?
qa.a: Asking to meet the manager the next morning; Kalyani should tell the truth, correct the claims and put the money back, before being found out.

qa.q: How might colleagues who round up see it if they heard this?
qa.a: They might feel uneasy, recognising how everyone does it makes a first small step feel normal and later ones easier.

grounding: Shows an employee who fudges an expense, calling it borrowing and telling themselves everyone does it, and finds each later step easier.

passage:
Dear Minakshi didi,
I'm writing this because I can't say it out loud yet.
You know about the loan for Papa's shop, and that my branch has missed its target three months running. The area manager said one more miss and I'm out. Last month I noticed that returned stock wasn't being checked by anyone. I marked some returns as sold. It made the numbers. Just once, I told myself. The company made crores last year; it won't even notice.
Didi, I've never taken even an extra samosa from the canteen. I always thought people who did this were a different kind of person. Now I lie awake doing sums in my head, and I understand how it starts. Not as thieves. As tired people with a good excuse.
I'm going to tell my regional head on Monday and correct the entries. Will you come with me to see a lawyer first, on Saturday? I'm scared, but I'm more scared of doing it again.
Ramesh

qa.q: What did Ramesh notice about returned stock?
qa.a: That returned stock wasn't being checked by anyone.

qa.q: How is Ramesh feeling while writing?
qa.a: Ramesh feels scared and ashamed, lying awake, shaken that someone who never took an extra samosa could do this.

qa.q: What steps is Ramesh planning, and why are they wise?
qa.a: Seeing a lawyer on Saturday, then telling the regional head and correcting the entries on Monday; coming forward early limits the harm.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Minakshi may feel shocked and worried, but also moved that Ramesh trusts Minakshi enough to ask for help.

grounding: Shows a person under targets and debt who uses a gap in checks with excuses such as the company can afford it, while still seeing themselves as honest.

passage: On the fourteenth floor of the Salt Lake office, Zeenat noticed it again at month-end: a round "adjustment" in the vendor account, approved by Mr Sen, with no invoice attached. It was the fourth month in a row. When internal audit emailed to schedule a visit, Mr Sen postponed it, twice, saying the team was too busy. Zeenat mentioned it to Trisha over lunch. Trisha shrugged. "He's the boss. And he just bought a new car. Maybe business is good. Don't get involved." Zeenat pushed rice around her plate. Maybe there was an innocent reason. She didn't want to accuse anyone. But four blank entries and two postponed audits weren't nothing. That evening she wrote down dates and amounts, only what she had seen, no guesses about motives. On Thursday she used the company's confidential ethics line, as the handbook said, and asked compliance to look. She felt sick sending it, and then, strangely, lighter.

qa.q: How many times did Mr Sen postpone the audit?
qa.a: Twice.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel about raising the issue?
qa.a: Zeenat felt uneasy and torn, not wanting to accuse anyone, then sick while sending the report and afterwards lighter.

qa.q: What made Zeenat's report careful and fair?
qa.a: She recorded only the dates and amounts she had seen, made no guesses about motives, and used the confidential ethics line as the handbook said.

qa.q: Why might Trisha prefer not to get involved?
qa.a: Trisha may feel uneasy about crossing the boss and want to avoid trouble, so she reaches for an innocent explanation.

grounding: Shows a team member noticing repeated odd adjustments and a boss who delays audits, and raising the doubt early through the proper channel.

passage: I sit across from Hafsa in the accounts section, so I saw most of it, though I can only guess what was going on inside her. For about a week in October she was quieter than usual. She'd stare at one spreadsheet for ages, close it, open it again. Once I saw her wipe her eyes quickly at her desk. On the Friday she printed something, stood up, sat down, and stood up again. Then she walked straight into the cabin of Joseph sir, the finance director, and closed the door. She was in there almost an hour. Later the office heard, in bits, that she had moved some figures between quarters to hide a shortfall in her project, and had come to correct it herself before the audit. Joseph sir called it a serious mistake and a brave correction. She wasn't fired; she lost her bonus and must have a senior sign off her entries for a year. She looks tired. She also looks like she's sleeping again.

qa.q: What did Hafsa do on the Friday?
qa.a: She walked into the cabin of Joseph sir, the finance director, closed the door and stayed almost an hour.

qa.q: What might Hafsa have been feeling during the quiet week?
qa.a: Hafsa seemed troubled and anxious, staring at the spreadsheet and wiping her eyes, perhaps torn about whether to come forward.

qa.q: Why was going to Joseph sir before the audit wise?
qa.a: Coming forward and correcting the record herself cost a bonus and a year of extra checks, far less than being found out later.

qa.q: How does the colleague telling the story see Hafsa now?
qa.a: The colleague sees Hafsa as tired but more at peace, noticing she looks like she's sleeping again.

grounding: Shows a person who took a wrong step, stopped, corrected the record and went to a senior before being found out, at a smaller cost.
